title: Differential headwise quantization fence + adaptive prefill scheduling for reduced dequant overhead
creator: Grace Chen
description:
Problem:
Current prefill + decode paths incur significant per-token dequantization cost when switching between INT8/FP8 kernel variants and mixed-precision kernels. This is especially visible on streaming decodes where small microbatches cause repeated dequant ops on KV cache slices. Existing approaches (layer-granular dequant scheduling or global eager dequant) either pay too much up-front cost or cause latency spikes during decode.

Goal:
Design and implement a runtime mechanism that: (1) reduces unnecessary dequant work by making dequantization decisions at head/granularity rather than layer-only; (2) schedules prefill microbatches to maximize reuse of quantized KV slices; (3) makes kernel selection adaptive at runtime based on telemetry (sequence length, head reuse, cache hit probability) so we pick the lowest-latency, quantization-friendly kernel variant without hurting output quality. Target: reduce dequant-related CPU/GPU time on average by ~25-35% for streaming workloads and improve P50 token latency by ~10%, while keeping quality regression <= 0.3% perplexity on eval set.

Design overview:
- "Quantization fence" concept: per-layer, per-head policy object that records whether a head's KV cache remains in quantized form across the next N tokens (head retention window). If retention probability > threshold, we keep that head in quantized form and route attention compute to int8-fused microkernels that avoid per-token dequant.
- Headwise telemetry: augment serving runtime telemetry with head-level reuse stats (hit probability, average reuse length, recent promotion/demotion events). Telemetry is kept lightweight (integer counters, EWMA) and aggregated at request boundary.
- Adaptive prefill scheduler: the prefill pipeline groups tokens into microbatches aligned with predicted head retention boundaries (prefill-aligned microbatching). This increases the amortization of any required dequant operations across a larger contiguous KV range.
- Kernel sweet-spot selection: at decision time we evaluate three candidates per attention op: int8-fused headwise kernel, mixed-precision kernel (fp16/float32 on QKV), and fallback dequant-then-fp16 kernel. Selection uses a small cost model combining measured latency samples, current occupancy, and retention probability.
- Safe fallback and guardrails: every decision is reversible within the same request. If a head's retention falls below threshold mid-request, we perform a controlled demotion (dequant + copy) on the next prefetch boundary and fall back to fp16 kernel for subsequent tokens. All transitions are recorded in trace logs for post-mortem and telemetry.

Implementation plan (high level tasks):
1) Runtime telemetry: add head-level counters and EWMA windows (ENG changes).
2) Quantization fence state machine: new runtime data structure, serialization for canary traces.
3) Kernel adapter: expose int8-fused headwise kernels with a narrow API surface; add selection hook for runtime cost model.
4) Prefill scheduler changes: modify microbatch creation to consider predicted retention windows.
5) Cost model: implement a compact decision function used inline by scheduler.
6) Tests & benchmarks: unit + integration + load tests + golden evals.
7) Rollout: feature-flag behind runtime-1.22, canary on internal cluster, gradual ramp to production.

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end integration passes nightly stability run on internal perf cluster.
- Streaming decode P50 latency improves >=10% and dequant-cost component decreases >=25% on a representative Reuters/LLM streaming benchmark.
- Token-level quality on our eval prompt set (1000 prompts) remains within 0.3% perplexity relative to baseline.
- No increase in OOM incidents or tail latency regressions beyond noise.
- Telemetry traces and transition logs are present and searchable in the console.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Headwise bookkeeping increases memory pressure. Mitigation: compact state (uint8 counters, capped EWMA) and sampling; enable only for models > 4B by default.
- Risk: Wrong predictions cause extra work and oscillations. Mitigation: hysteresis in retention thresholds, minimum time windows, and per-request reversal limits.
- Risk: Kernel bugs in new int8-fused path. Mitigation: staged hardware tests, CPU reference implementation, and exhaustive FP32 comparison fuzz tests.

Measurement plan:
- Add perf counters: dequant_ops_count, dequant_time_ms, head_retention_rate, kernel_choice_rate.
- Dashboards: per-model, per-route breakdown of dequant delta pre/post rollout.
- SLOs: monitor p99/p999 latency and error rates during canary.

Artifacts and links:
- Design spec (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Quant+Fence+Design
- Proto PR (WIP): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4128
- Kernel harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kernel-harness/tree/feature/headwise-int8
- Perf dashboard (internal): https://dashboards.redwood.ai/d/prefill/quant-fence-canary

Notes: this intentionally targets head granularity because attention head reuse patterns vary widely between autoregressive and seq2seq workloads; layer-only decisions leave 40-60% of opportunities unused based on our sampling. The approach should be model-agnostic and exposed as opt-in per-route configuration in later work.
